stem: When teaching malignancy-prevention measures after transplantation, which sun-exposure guidance aligns with standard references?

options.text: Use tanning beds daily to improve vitamin D without risk
Tanning beds are safer than outdoor sun for transplant recipients
Tanning beds are recommended instead of sunscreen

explanation.rationale_correct: Cancer-prevention teaching includes sun precautions such as avoiding undue sunlight exposure and avoiding tanning beds, along with protective clothing and sunscreen.

rationale_incorrect.B: Tanning beds are avoided rather than used daily for vitamin D.
rationale_incorrect.C: Tanning beds are not described as safer than outdoor sun exposure.
rationale_incorrect.D: Sunscreen and sun avoidance are recommended rather than tanning beds.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 6, Noninfectious Diseases → Prevention of cancer → Sun precautions

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 6 → Prevention of cancer → 4.b. (avoid tanning beds); PDF p. 282 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Tanning-bed avoidance angle distinct from SPF greater than 50 teaching (cctc-1103) and hepatitis B HCC prevention (cctc-1112); anchor verified on Cupples p. 282.

stem: A transplant recipient on cyclosporine develops elevated lipids. Which long-term management approach aligns with standard references?

options.text: Medications, dietary changes, and exercise as indicated
No treatment because immunosuppression prevents hyperlipidemia
Complete dietary fat elimination with no exercise or medications
Defer all lipid management until twenty years post-transplant

explanation.rationale_correct: Hyperlipidemia may develop as a side effect of immunosuppressive medications and may be managed with medications, dietary changes, and exercise.

rationale_incorrect.B: Immunosuppressants can cause hyperlipidemia rather than preventing it.
rationale_incorrect.C: Management includes medications and exercise in addition to dietary modification.
rationale_incorrect.D: Lipid management begins when hyperlipidemia develops rather than being deferred for decades.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 3, Patient Education → j. Long-term effects of immunosuppression → iii. Hyperlipidemia
primary_anchor.quote_hint: May be managed with medications … dietary changes, and exercise

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 3 → j. Long-term effects of immunosuppression → iii. Hyperlipidemia (medications, diet, exercise); PDF p. 120 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Hyperlipidemia lifestyle-management angle distinct from sirolimus hyperlipidemia adverse effect (cctc-3077) and long-term IS combo (cctc-1038); anchor verified on Cupples p. 120.

stem: When teaching animal-safety precautions after transplantation, which pet-care guidance aligns with standard references?

options.text: Keep pets immunized and in good health
Household pets require no vaccinations after transplant
Pet health is unrelated to transplant infection risk

explanation.rationale_correct: Animal-safety teaching includes keeping pets immunized and in good health, along with precautions for litter, fecal matter, and new pets.

rationale_incorrect.B: Pet immunization and health maintenance are recommended for household pets.
rationale_incorrect.C: Household pets should be immunized and healthy, not only stray animals.
rationale_incorrect.D: Pet-related exposures can transmit infection to immunosuppressed recipients.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 3, Patient Education → e. Infection prevention → v. Animal safety
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Keep pets immunized and in good health

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 3 → e. Infection prevention → v. Animal safety (keep pets immunized and in good health); PDF p. 116 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Pet-immunization angle distinct from cat-litter precautions (cctc-1099) and new-pet timing (cctc-1100); anchor verified on Cupples p. 116.

stem: A coordinator is updating animal-safety infection-prevention teaching. Evaluate the following statements:

elements.text: Recipients should avoid handling cat litter when possible because bacteria may become airborne.
If cat litter handling is unavoidable, disposable gloves and a surgical mask should be used.
Recipients should avoid contact with pets that have diarrhea.
Stray animals may be petted freely because bites and scratches never transmit infection.

explanation.rationale_correct: Teaching includes avoiding cat litter and fecal matter when possible, using gloves and a mask if unavoidable, and avoiding pets with diarrhea. Stray animals should be avoided because they may bite or scratch.

rationale_incorrect.A: Statement III is also true—contact with pets with diarrhea should be avoided.
rationale_incorrect.C: Statement I is also true; statement IV is false.
rationale_incorrect.D: Statement IV is false because stray animals may bite or scratch and should not be petted.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 3, Patient Education → e. Infection prevention → v. Animal safety
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Avoid handling fecal matter especially cat litter … wear gloves … surgical mask … Avoid contact with pets … with diarrhea … Avoid stray animals

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 3 → e. Infection prevention → v. Animal safety (litter, gloves/mask, diarrhea, stray animals); PDF p. 116 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Animal-safety combo distinct from pet-immunization recall (cctc-1116) and visitor-precaution combo (cctc-1113); anchor verified on Cupples p. 116.
